plants.identification:
Ajwain is a small annual aromatic herb with finely divided leaves and small white flowers
arranged in umbrella-shaped clusters. Its fruits are small, oval and greyish-brown, with
prominent ridges. They have a strong, characteristic aroma and a pungent, thyme-like taste.
The characteristic smell is mainly associated with its essential oil.
traditionalReferences:
Ajwain is traditionally known by names such as Yavānī and Ajmodā.
• Classical Ayurvedic texts describe aromatic and pungent substances used in digestive
preparations.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu describes Yavānī and its traditional properties.
• Ajwain occurs in various traditional compound formulations, particularly those
associated with digestion and abdominal discomfort.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Indigestion
• Gas and abdominal bloating
• Abdominal discomfort
• Loss of appetite
• Digestive weakness
• Certain respiratory complaints
• As a warming aromatic ingredient in formulations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Ajwain has been investigated experimentally for antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-
inflammatory and digestive-related effects.
Its essential oil has shown antimicrobial activity in laboratory studies. Animal and laboratory
research has also investigated its possible effects on gastrointestinal function and inflammation.
However, much of the evidence remains preclinical, meaning that laboratory or animal findings
cannot automatically be applied to humans.
knownCompounds:
Ajwain contains:
• Thymol
• Carvacrol
• p-Cymene
• γ-Terpinene
• α-Pinene
• Other volatile-oil constituents
Thymol is particularly important because it contributes strongly to ajwain's aroma and biological
activity.
plants.safetySummary:
Ajwain consumed as a culinary spice is generally well tolerated. Concentrated essential oil is
much stronger and may cause irritation if used improperly. Large medicinal quantities should not
be treated as equivalent to normal dietary consumption.

plants.identification:
Agnimantha is a large shrub or small tree with hairy branches. Leaves are generally ovate to
triangular and may have entire or somewhat toothed margins. The flowers are small, fragrant and
generally white to pinkish, occurring in clusters.
The plant is adapted to relatively dry and tropical regions.
traditionalReferences:
Charaka Saṃhitā
Agnimantha is associated with:
• Dashamula
• Śirovirecanopaga
• Śothahara
The Dashamula group is explicitly listed in Charaka's Siddhi Sthāna context.
Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu
Gudūcyādi Varga — verse 24 is cited for Agnimantha's properties.
The classical description gives it properties including:
• Katu
• Tikta
• Kashaya
• Madhura
• Ushna
and associates it traditionally with Vata-Kapha disorders, swelling and impaired digestion.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in contexts involving:
• Shotha — swelling/inflammatory conditions
• Vata disorders
• Joint and musculoskeletal complaints
• Digestive weakness
• Fever
• Certain metabolic disorders
• Conditions associated with Kapha accumulation
scientificEvidence:
Experimental studies on Clerodendrum phlomidis have investigated anti-inflammatory and
hypoglycaemic/hypolipidaemic activities.
Animal and laboratory studies have reported reduction of experimentally induced inflammation
and changes in glucose/lipid parameters. However, these findings do not establish clinical
efficacy in humans.
knownCompounds:
Reported phytochemical groups include:
• Flavonoids
• Phenolic compounds
• Terpenoids
• Sterols
• Iridoid-related constituents
plants.safetySummary:
Human clinical safety data are limited. Concentrated extracts should not be considered
equivalent to traditional formulations simply because the plant has a long history of use.

plants.identification:
Aloe vera is a succulent perennial plant with thick, fleshy, lance-shaped leaves arranged in a
rosette. The leaves have a green to grey-green colour and small teeth along their margins. The
inner part of the leaf contains a clear gel, while the outer leaf contains latex.
traditionalReferences:
Aloe vera is known in Ayurveda mainly as Kumārī. Unlike herbs that occur prominently in the
earliest Saṃhitās, Kumārī is more clearly described in later Ayurvedic literature.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu — describes Kumārī and its properties.
• Classical Ayurvedic literature and later compendia describe Kumārī in various medicinal
preparations.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Aloe vera has been used in Ayurvedic preparations in contexts related to:
• Skin-related conditions
• Wounds and burns
• Digestive complaints
• Certain liver-related conditions
• Women's health-related preparations
• General medicinal formulations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research has investigated Aloe vera particularly for topical skin and wound applications.
Several clinical reviews have reported possible benefits in wound healing, including burns,
although results across studies are not completely consistent. A 2024 systematic review and
meta-analysis of randomized trials found that topical Aloe vera reduced healing time in burn
injuries, while its effect on pain and infection remained uncertain.
plants.safetySummary:
Topical Aloe vera gel is generally well tolerated, but burning, itching, rash or eczema can
occasionally occur. Oral Aloe latex may cause abdominal cramps and diarrhea, and oral Aloe
products require greater caution.

plants.identification:
Amla is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree with a straight trunk and a spreading crown. Its
leaves are small, simple and closely arranged along slender branchlets, giving them a feathery
appearance. The flowers are small and greenish-yellow. Its fruit is round, smooth and pale
greenish-yellow, with characteristic vertical ridges and a hard stone containing seeds.
traditionalReferences: Amla is known as Āmalakī and Dhātrī in classical Ayurvedic literature.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Amla has been used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Digestive health
• General nourishment and rejuvenation
• Respiratory complaints
• Hair and scalp preparations
• Eye-related health
• Skin-related conditions
• Liver-related traditional preparations
• General weakness and convalescence
• As an ingredient in classical formulations such as Triphala and Chyavanaprāśa
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments or cures.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research on Phyllanthus emblica has particularly investigated its antioxidant, metabolic,
cardiovascular and other biological effects.
Antioxidant activity: Amla fruit is rich in vitamin C and various polyphenolic compounds.
Laboratory and experimental studies have demonstrated antioxidant activity in extracts of the
fruit.
Metabolic health: Clinical studies have investigated standardized Amla preparations in people
with abnormal lipid profiles and metabolic risk factors. Some studies have reported
improvements in cholesterol and triglyceride measures, although the number of participants and
duration of studies have generally been limited.
Cardiovascular risk: Some human studies have reported potentially beneficial effects of Amla
preparations on lipid profiles and markers associated with cardiovascular risk.
Evidence limitation: Human clinical research on Amla is still relatively limited. Studies use
different extracts, doses and preparations, making results difficult to compare. Therefore, current
evidence does not establish Amla as a treatment or cure for disease.
plants.safetySummary:
Amla fruit is traditionally consumed as food and is generally considered well tolerated in normal
dietary amounts.
However, concentrated extracts and supplements are different from ordinary food consumption.
Their effects can vary depending on dose and preparation. People taking medicines or using
concentrated Amla supplements should seek appropriate medical advice, particularly because
Amla may potentially influence blood glucose, blood lipids or blood clotting.

plants.identification:
Apamarga is an erect herb with a rough, hairy stem. Leaves are opposite, oval to ovate and
covered with fine hairs.
Its most recognizable feature is the long terminal flower spike. The flowers are small and
greenish, and the stiff bracts become prickly and easily attach to animals or clothing.
This characteristic helps explain its traditional name and method of dispersal.
traditionalReferences:
Apamarga has extensive classical references.
Important references include:
• Charaka Saṃhitā, Sūtra Sthāna 4/9(23) — Vamanopaga Mahākaṣāya
• Sūtra Sthāna 25/40 — Agrya reference
• Vimāna Sthāna 6/17 — Krimi-related use
• Vimāna Sthāna 8/135 — Vamana drugs
• Kalpa Sthāna 1/14 — Vamana
• Chikitsā Sthāna 9/66 — Nasya and Anjana applications
traditionalUses:
Traditionally associated with:
• Krimi-related disorders
• Digestive complaints
• Vamana preparations
• Nasya
• Traditional management of piles
• Skin conditions
• Swelling
• External applications
• Certain respiratory preparations
scientificEvidence:
Experimental studies have investigated Apamarga for:
• Antioxidant effects
• Anti-inflammatory effects
• Antimicrobial activity
• Immunomodulatory effects
• Possible analgesic activity
However, most evidence remains laboratory- or animal-based, and human clinical research is
comparatively limited.
knownCompounds:
Reported constituents include:
• Triterpenoid saponins
• Ecdysterone
• Flavonoids
• Alkaloids
• Sterols
• Polysaccharides
• Long-chain fatty compounds
plants.safetySummary:
Apamarga is traditionally used in procedures such as Vamana and Nasya, but these are
specialized Ayurvedic procedures and should not be attempted at home.

plants.identification:
Aparajita is a perennial climbing herb. It has compound leaves and attractive pea-shaped flowers,
most commonly deep blue, though white varieties also occur.
The flowers have a characteristic butterfly/pea-flower shape.
traditionalReferences:
Charaka Saṃhitā
The Charaka database records Aparajita in:
• Sūtra Sthāna 1/77 — Śirovirechana
• Sūtra Sthāna 2/4 — Śirovirechana
• Sūtra Sthāna 5/26 — Vairecanika Dhūma
• Cikitsā Sthāna 23/95
• Cikitsā Sthāna 23/195
• Cikitsā Sthāna 23/210
• Cikitsā Sthāna 26/69
• Cikitsā Sthāna 30/91
Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu
The cited verse describing Aparajita is:
Verse 97
It describes the plant as:
• Katu
• Tikta
• Sheeta
• Medhya
• Kaṇṭhya
and traditionally associates it with Kuṣṭha, urinary disorders, Tridoṣa conditions, swelling,
wounds and poisoning.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in contexts involving:
• Memory/intellectual functions
• Throat-related preparations
• Skin disorders
• Swelling
• Wounds
• Poison-related formulations
• Head-related therapies
scientificEvidence:
Modern research has investigated Clitoria ternatea for:
• Antioxidant activity
• Cognitive/neuroprotective potential
• Anti-inflammatory activity
• Antidiabetic activity
• Antimicrobial activity
Some animal and laboratory studies report cognitive and antioxidant effects, but human clinical
evidence remains insufficient to establish it as a treatment for memory disorders.
knownCompounds:
Especially important are:
• Ternatins
• Anthocyanins
• Flavonoids
• Kaempferol
• Quercetin
• Phenolic compounds
The blue flower colour is largely associated with polyacylated anthocyanins called ternatins.
plants.safetySummary:
Food-level use and concentrated medicinal extracts are not necessarily equivalent.
Standardization and dosage are important.

plants.scientificName: Terminalia arjuna (Roxb. ex DC.) Wight & Arn.
plants.identification:
Arjuna is a large deciduous tree that can grow to considerable height. It has a characteristic
smooth, grey outer bark and a broad spreading crown. The leaves are simple and oblong, while
the tree produces small flowers and fruits with characteristic ridges.
traditionalReferences:
Arjuna is a well-known medicinal tree in Ayurveda and is particularly associated with traditional
preparations involving the heart and cardiovascular system.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Arjuna has been used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Heart health
• Cardiovascular complaints
• General strength and nourishment
• Wound-related preparations
• Respiratory and other traditional medicinal applications
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research on Terminalia arjuna has particularly investigated its possible
cardioprotective, antioxidant and cardiovascular effects.
Cardiovascular research: Reviews of preclinical and clinical studies have reported
investigations into possible effects including antioxidant, hypotensive, anti-inflammatory and
other cardiovascular activities.
Clinical evidence: Human studies have investigated Arjuna bark preparations in cardiovascular
conditions, including coronary artery disease. However, studies vary considerably in their
preparations, doses and designs.
Evidence limitation: Although laboratory, animal and some human studies provide promising
findings, the evidence is not sufficient to consider Arjuna a replacement for standard
cardiovascular treatment. Further high-quality clinical research is required.
knownCompounds:
Arjuna bark contains several bioactive compounds, including:
• Triterpenoids
• Flavonoids
• Tannins
• Glycosides
• Phenolic compounds
These phytochemicals are being studied for their possible antioxidant and cardiovascular
biological activities.
plants.safetySummary:
Arjuna has a long history of traditional use, and research has generally reported acceptable
tolerability in studied preparations. However, safety data are not sufficient to assume that all
concentrated extracts are risk-free.
Because Arjuna may have cardiovascular effects, people with heart conditions or those taking
cardiovascular medicines should seek appropriate medical advice before using concentrated
preparations. Potential drug interactions and long-term safety require further study.

plants.identification:
Arka is a hardy shrub with thick, opposite, grey-green leaves. The leaves and stems produce a
characteristic white milky latex when damaged.
Flowers are waxy and generally white, pale purple or violet. The plant produces large follicles
containing numerous seeds with silky hairs that help wind dispersal.
traditionalReferences:
Charaka Saṃhitā includes Arka in several classifications and procedures:
• Sūtra Sthāna 4/9(4) — Bhedanīya Mahākaṣāya
• Sūtra Sthāna 4/9(22) — Svedopaga Mahākaṣāya
• Sūtra Sthāna 14/31 — Nāḍī Sveda
• Sūtra Sthāna 14/42 — Prastara Sveda
• Sūtra Sthāna 27 — references in Dravyas
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in carefully prepared formulations associated with:
• Vāta-related conditions
• Digestive disorders
• Svedana
• External applications
• Certain skin-related preparations
• Traditional Śodhana procedures
scientificEvidence:
Modern studies have investigated Calotropis procera for:
• Anti-inflammatory activity
• Antioxidant activity
• Antimicrobial activity
• Analgesic activity
• Other pharmacological effects
The plant contains cardiac glycosides and other potent compounds, making interpretation of
experimental research particularly important.
knownCompounds:
• Calotropin
• Calotoxin
• Uscharin
• Calactin
• Cardiac glycosides
• Flavonoids
• Terpenoids
• Proteolytic enzymes
plants.safetySummary:
Arka should NOT be recommended as a DIY medicinal plant.
Its latex can cause:
• Skin irritation
• Eye irritation
• Inflammation
• Severe eye injury
• Toxic effects if swallowed
The app should display:
⚠️ CAUTION: Potent medicinal and potentially toxic plant — professional preparation
required.

plants.identification:
Ashoka is an evergreen tree that can grow approximately 6–10 metres or more. It has a dense,
spreading crown and compound leaves with elongated leaflets.
Its flowers are highly distinctive, appearing in dense clusters. They change colour as they
mature, commonly progressing from yellowish or orange shades toward reddish tones. The tree
produces flat pods containing several seeds.
Important identification note: The medicinal Ashoka of Ayurveda, Saraca asoca, should not
be confused with the commonly planted false Ashoka (Polyalthia longifolia).
partsUsed: Stem bark; flowers and other parts are also used
traditionalReferences:
Ashoka is traditionally known as Aśoka.
• Charaka Saṃhitā mentions medicinal substances used in women's health-related
preparations, although Ashoka's prominence becomes clearer in later Ayurvedic
literature.
• Suśruta Saṃhitā and later Ayurvedic texts describe Ashoka in medicinal contexts.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu provides a detailed description of Aśoka.
• Ashoka bark is especially prominent in later Ayurvedic formulations associated with
gynecological health.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Menstrual discomfort
• Excessive menstrual bleeding
• Uterine and gynecological preparations
• Women's reproductive health
• Inflammatory conditions
• Certain digestive and general medicinal preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research has investigated Saraca asoca for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory,
antimicrobial and reproductive-system-related biological activities.
Laboratory and animal studies have reported biological effects from bark and other extracts.
However, high-quality human clinical evidence for many traditional gynecological uses remains
limited.
This is particularly important for your app: traditional use should not be converted into a
statement that Ashoka treats menstrual or reproductive disorders.
knownCompounds:
Ashoka contains:
• Catechin
• Epicatechin
• Procyanidins
• Quercetin
• Kaempferol
• Tannins
• Various flavonoids and phenolic compounds
plants.safetySummary:
Ashoka has a long history of traditional use, but safety data for concentrated extracts are less
extensive than for ordinary food plants. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, existing medical conditions
and concurrent medications warrant particular caution with medicinal preparations.

plants.identification:
Ashwagandha is a small, branched shrub with oval leaves and small greenish-yellow flowers. It
produces small red-orange berries. The roots have a characteristic smell.
traditionalReferences:
Ashwagandha is described in classical Ayurvedic literature, including Charaka Saṃhitā and Suśruta
Saṃhitā. It is traditionally classified among Rasāyana plants
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Ashwagandha root preparations have been used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Strength and physical nourishment
• General weakness
• Supporting healthy sleep
• Stress and mental well-being
• Rasāyana (traditional rejuvenative practices)
l 5. Scientific Evidence
Clinical studies suggest that standardized Ashwagandha extracts may help reduce stress and
anxiety and may modestly improve sleep, but further high-quality research is required to
establish definitive clinical benefits
Stress & anxiety: A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 9 randomized controlled
trials (558 participants) found that Ashwagandha preparations significantly reduced
Perceived Stress Scale scores, Hamilton Anxiety scores, and serum cortisol compared
with placebo.
Sleep: A meta-analysis of 5 randomized controlled trials (400 adults) found a small but
statistically significant improvement in overall sleep, with greater effects reported in
adults with insomnia and in studies using ≥600 mg/day for ≥8 weeks.
Cortisol: A systematic review of 9 human studies found that Ashwagandha
supplementation generally reduced cortisol in stressed participants, although the studies
differed in dose, preparation and duration.
Active compounds: Ashwagandha contains withanolides, a group of steroidal lactones
being investigated for biological effects. However, the exact mechanisms responsible for its
effects in humans are not yet fully established.
plants.safetySummary:
Ashwagandha is not automatically safe just because it is a plant. Some people can experience side
effects, and there are reported concerns involving liver injury and interactions with medicines. The app
should therefore include a safety warning and avoid recommending self-medication
Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is a medicinal plant traditionally used in Ayurveda,
particularly its root. Ancient Ayurvedic texts describe it in the context of strengthening and
Rasāyana practices. Modern research has investigated compounds such as withanolides and their
possible effects on stress, sleep and physical performance. Traditional uses should be
distinguished from scientifically established medical effects.

plants.identification:
Atibala is a soft, hairy herb or shrub. The stem is branched and covered with fine hairs. Leaves
are broadly ovate to heart-shaped, with serrated margins and a velvety texture.
The flowers are generally yellow and arise singly from the leaf axils. The fruit is distinctive,
consisting of numerous small segments arranged around a central axis.
The plant is commonly found in wastelands, roadsides, agricultural areas and other disturbed
habitats in tropical and subtropical regions.
traditionalReferences:
Atibala is specifically mentioned in classical Ayurvedic sources.
Important Charaka references include:
• Sūtra Sthāna 4/9(7) — Balya Mahākaṣāya
• Vimāna Sthāna 8/139 — Madhura Skandha
• Śārīra Sthāna 8/24 — Garbhiṇī Paricaryā
• Chikitsā Sthāna 1/2/4 — Amalaka Ghṛta
• Chikitsā Sthāna 29/56 — Balādi Ghṛta
• Chikitsā Sthāna 29/62 — Jīvanīya Ghṛta
Its classical descriptions associate it with nourishing and strengthening properties.
traditionalUses:
Atibala has traditionally been used in preparations associated with:
• Physical weakness
• General nourishment
• Vāta-Pitta imbalance
• Strength-promoting preparations
• Traditional rejuvenation
• Musculoskeletal support
• Certain reproductive-health formulations
• Ghṛta and taila preparations
It is generally used as part of a formulation rather than as an isolated treatment.
scientificEvidence:
Experimental studies on Abutilon indicum have reported:
• Antioxidant activity
• Anti-inflammatory activity
• Analgesic activity
• Antimicrobial activity
• Possible hepatoprotective and other biological effects
However, most evidence is preclinical, and relatively few high-quality human clinical studies
are available.
Therefore, these findings should be described in Jeevan Sutra as research findings rather than
confirmed medical treatments.
knownCompounds:
Reported constituents include:
• Flavonoids
• Alkaloids
• Phenolic compounds
• Sterols
• Fatty acids
• Mucilage
• Polysaccharides
• Other secondary metabolites
plants.safetySummary:
Traditional use provides useful historical information but does not establish the safety of every
concentrated extract.
Correct plant identification, appropriate preparation and professional guidance are important,
particularly for medicinal doses.

plants.identification:
Bael is a small to medium-sized tree that can reach approximately 10–15 metres. It often has
branches bearing sharp spines. Its leaves are usually trifoliate, with three leaflets arranged
together.
The tree produces fragrant greenish-white flowers. Its fruit is round or oval with a hard woody
shell. The mature fruit contains aromatic orange-yellow pulp with numerous seeds covered by
mucilaginous material.
traditionalReferences:
Bael is traditionally known as Bilva and is an important plant in classical Ayurveda.
• Charaka Saṃhitā includes Bilva among important medicinal groups and formulations.
• Suśruta Saṃhitā also describes Bilva.
• Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya gives Bilva an important place among medicinal plants.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu provides descriptions of its properties and different plant parts
used traditionally.
Bilva is also one of the plants associated with the Daśamūla group in classical Ayurveda.
traditionalUses:
Different parts of Bilva have traditionally been used in contexts related to:
• Digestive complaints
• Diarrhea and intestinal disturbances
• Loss of appetite
• Abdominal discomfort
• Respiratory complaints
• Inflammatory conditions
• General restorative preparations
The unripe and ripe fruits have traditionally been used differently in Ayurvedic preparations.
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Modern studies of Aegle marmelos have investigated antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-
inflammatory and gastrointestinal-related activities.
Fruit preparations have received particular scientific interest because of their nutritional and
phytochemical composition. Laboratory and animal studies suggest several biological effects, but
clinical evidence in humans remains limited for many traditional indications.
knownCompounds:
Bael contains:
• Marmelosin
• Aegeline
• Skimmianine
• Imperatorin
• Tannins
• Flavonoids
• Coumarins
• Various volatile compounds
The chemical composition varies considerably between different plant parts and stages of fruit
maturity.
plants.safetySummary:
Bael fruit is traditionally consumed as food, but medicinal preparations made from concentrated
extracts may have different effects. Excessive intake of unripe fruit preparations may cause
digestive effects such as constipation in some individuals.
People using concentrated preparations or medicines should seek appropriate professional
advice.

plants.identification:
Bala is a small erect herb or undershrub that may become approximately 1–2 metres tall. The
stems are branched and covered with fine hairs. Leaves are generally heart-shaped or ovate, with
serrated margins and a soft, slightly rough texture.
The flowers are small and usually yellow or pale yellow, occurring singly or in small groups.
The fruit is a segmented schizocarp consisting of several small wedge-shaped parts.
Because several Sida species can look similar, correct botanical identification is important
when collecting or preparing the plant.
traditionalReferences:
Bala is repeatedly mentioned in classical Ayurvedic literature.
Important references include:
• Charaka Saṃhitā, Sūtra Sthāna 4/9(7) — included in Balya Mahākaṣāya, a group of
drugs traditionally associated with promoting strength.
• Sūtra Sthāna 4/9(2) — associated with Brimhaṇīya Mahākaṣāya, relating to
nourishment.
• Classical Ayurvedic texts also discuss Bala in preparations concerned with Vāta
disorders, weakness and rejuvenation.
• Later Nighaṇṭu literature provides descriptions of its rasa, guṇa, vīrya and traditional
actions.
Ayurvedic descriptions generally associate Bala with Madhura rasa, Guru and Snigdha
qualities and a nourishing action.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Bala has been included in preparations used for:
• General physical weakness and debility
• Supporting strength and nourishment
• Vāta-dominant disorders
• Musculoskeletal discomfort and stiffness
• Traditional strengthening formulations
• Recovery after weakness
• Rasāyana-oriented preparations
• Traditional oil preparations used externally
Bala is also frequently included in classical formulations containing several strengthening herbs
rather than being used alone.
These are traditional Ayurvedic uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research on Sida cordifolia has investigated its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory,
analgesic, antimicrobial and other pharmacological properties.
Much of this research comes from laboratory and animal experiments. Therefore, evidence
showing a biological effect in an experimental model cannot automatically be interpreted as
proof that the plant treats a disease in humans.
Another important scientific consideration is the variation in chemical composition between
different Sida species and preparations. This makes proper botanical identification and
standardized extracts especially important.
knownCompounds:
Reported phytochemicals include:
• Ephedrine-type alkaloids
• Vasicinol
• Choline
• Phenethylamine-related compounds
• Flavonoids
• Phytosterols
• Phenolic compounds
• Fatty acids
• Phytoecdysteroids
The concentration of these compounds can vary according to plant part, geographical origin and
extraction method.

plants.identification:
Bakula is an evergreen tree with dense foliage. Its small, white, strongly fragrant flowers are one
of its most characteristic features.
The fruits are fleshy berries that become yellowish-orange to reddish when mature.
traditionalReferences:
Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu
Puṣpa Varga — verse 33
The verse describes Bakula as:
• Tuvara
• Anuṣṇa
• Guru
• Katu-vipaka
and traditionally associates it with Kapha-Pitta disorders, poisoning, skin disorders, worms
and dental diseases.
Bakula is also classically valued in oral and dental care.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally associated with:
• Dental disorders
• Gum problems
• Oral hygiene

plants.identification:
Brahmi is a small, creeping, succulent herb commonly found in moist and marshy environments.
It has fleshy, oval leaves arranged along its stems and produces small, usually white flowers with
distinctive markings.
traditionalReferences:
Brahmi is described in Ayurvedic literature in connection with medhya (intellect-supporting)
and memory-related uses.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Brahmi has been used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Memory and learning
• Concentration and mental function
• Mental fatigue
• Nervous-system-related complaints
• Stress and restlessness
• General cognitive support
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research on Bacopa monnieri has particularly investigated its possible effects on
memory and cognitive function.
Memory: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 76 adults aged 40–65
years, Bacopa supplementation was investigated over a longer period and showed effects on
some aspects of memory.
Cognitive function: A randomized placebo-controlled trial involving 60 medical students found
statistically significant improvements in several cognitive-function tests after six weeks of
standardized Bacopa extract.
Recent evidence: A 2025 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study involving 101
adults found that Bacopa extract did not significantly improve its primary measures of verbal
learning, attention or working memory, although reductions in self-reported stress reactivity and
some fatigue/stress measures were observed.
Evidence limitation: Human studies have used different extracts, doses, durations and
populations. Therefore, current research suggests potential cognitive effects but does not
establish Brahmi as a treatment or cure for neurological or psychological diseases.
knownCompounds:

• Bacosides
• Bacopasides
• Alkaloids
• Saponins
• Flavonoids
Bacosides are among the major compounds studied in relation to Brahmi's biological and
cognitive effects.
plants.safetySummary:
Brahmi has generally been well tolerated in human studies, but gastrointestinal effects such as
stomach upset have been reported. Concentrated extracts may differ from traditionally prepared
forms.
People taking medicines or using concentrated supplements should seek appropriate medical
advice. Evidence regarding long-term use and use during pregnancy or breastfeeding remains
limited.

similar to a compound leaf.

leaves, which is a distinctive identifying feature of the plant.

closely related species may be referred to by similar vernacular names. Correct botanical
identification is therefore important for your app.

Bhumyamalaki is traditionally known as Bhūmyāmalakī.

• Urinary complaints

scientificEvidence:

advice.

Charaka Saṃhitā contains numerous references to Eranda:

• Sūtra Sthāna 4/9(44) — Aṅgamarda-praśamana

Properly manufactured castor oil does not contain ricin in the same way because ricin is a protein

• Severe diarrhoea
• Dehydration
• Electrolyte imbalance

Dhatura is particularly important in later Ayurvedic Agada Tantra and Nighaṇṭu literature,
where poisonous medicinal plants are described along with their proper processing and
therapeutic limitations.

identification should be verified before assigning a particular Sanskrit reference to Datura metel.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally processed Dhatura has been used in specific formulations associated with:
• Pain
• Vāta-related disorders
• Respiratory complaints
• Certain skin conditions
• Spasmodic conditions
• External medicinal preparations

scientificEvidence:
Datura species contain powerful tropane alkaloids that act on muscarinic acetylcholine
receptors.
Modern pharmacology recognizes compounds such as atropine and scopolamine as potent
anticholinergic substances.
Research has investigated various pharmacological properties of Datura, but toxicity is a major
limitation.

produces yellow flowers arranged in umbrella-shaped clusters. Its elongated greenish or
brownish fruits have a characteristic sweet, anise-like aroma.

Fennel is traditionally known by names such as Śatapuṣpā and Madhurikā.

• Gas and bloating
• Abdominal discomfort
• Appetite and digestion

plants.identification:
Fenugreek is a small annual herb with three-parted leaves and small pale-yellow or whitish
flowers. Its long, narrow pods contain several hard, yellowish-brown seeds with a characteristic
bitter and aromatic taste.

Fenugreek is traditionally known as Methikā.

traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in contexts related to:

• Appetite and digestion
• General weakness
• Joint-related discomfort
• Skin-related preparations
• Women's health-related traditional preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Fenugreek has been studied more extensively than many traditional herbs. Research has
investigated its possible effects on blood glucose, cholesterol, inflammation and digestive
function. Some clinical trials suggest potential benefits for blood glucose control, but study
quality and results vary, so fenugreek should not replace prescribed diabetes treatment.

• 4-Hydroxyisoleucine

Fenugreek is commonly eaten as a food. Larger medicinal amounts may cause diarrhea, gas or
other digestive symptoms. It may also lower blood glucose and therefore can interact with
diabetes medicines. Allergic reactions are possible, particularly in people sensitive to legumes.

plants.identification:
Giloy is a large, climbing shrub with succulent, green, heart-shaped leaves and long aerial roots.
The stems are fleshy and often have a characteristic greyish, corky appearance when mature. It
produces small yellowish-green flowers, followed by small fruits that become red when mature.
traditionalReferences: Giloy is known as Guḍūcī and Amṛtā in classical Ayurvedic literature.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Giloy has been used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Fever
• Digestive complaints
• Loss of appetite
• General weakness and convalescence
• Inflammatory conditions
• Respiratory complaints
• Skin-related conditions
• Metabolic health
• General rejuvenative preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments or cures.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research on Tinospora cordifolia has investigated its immunomodulatory, antioxidant,
anti-inflammatory, metabolic and other biological effects.
Immune and inflammatory research: Laboratory and animal studies have reported effects of
different Giloy extracts on immune and inflammatory pathways. However, these findings cannot
by themselves establish clinical effectiveness in humans.
Metabolic health: Experimental and some clinical research has investigated Giloy in relation to
blood glucose and other metabolic measures. Evidence remains insufficient to establish it as a
treatment for diabetes or other metabolic diseases.
Liver safety: Although Giloy has a long history of traditional use, an important area of modern
research concerns reports of liver injury associated with some Giloy preparations. The
relationship may depend on factors such as preparation, dose and individual susceptibility, and
further research is needed.
Evidence limitation: Human clinical evidence for Giloy remains limited, and studies vary in
their extracts, doses and preparation methods. Therefore, Giloy should not be presented as a
proven treatment or cure for disease.
plants.safetySummary:
Giloy should not automatically be considered completely safe because it is a traditional or
natural medicine.
Although it has been traditionally used for a long time, published medical reports have described
cases of liver injury associated with Giloy (Tinospora cordifolia) preparations. The risk may
vary according to the preparation and individual factors.
Concentrated extracts and supplements should therefore be used cautiously. People with liver
problems, people taking medicines, pregnant people and children should seek appropriate
medical advice before using medicinal Giloy preparations.

plants.identification:
Ginger is a perennial herb with narrow, lance-shaped leaves arising from underground rhizomes.

formulations.

traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:

• Nausea
• Abdominal discomfort
• Cough and respiratory complaints
• Loss of appetite
• Joint and inflammatory complaints

scientificEvidence:
Ginger has been extensively studied in humans. Systematic reviews of randomized trials suggest
that ginger may be useful for certain types of nausea and vomiting, particularly pregnancy-
associated nausea. Research has also examined its effects on digestive function and
inflammatory conditions, although evidence quality differs between applications.

plants.safetySummary:
Ginger is commonly consumed as a food and is generally well tolerated. Higher supplemental
amounts may cause gastrointestinal discomfort, heartburn or irritation in some people.

plants.identification:
Gokshura is a low-growing, spreading herb with stems that grow along the ground. Its leaves are
divided into small paired leaflets.
The plant produces small yellow flowers. Its distinctive fruits are hard and covered with sharp
spines, allowing them to attach to animals and clothing for dispersal. This spiny fruit is
associated with its Sanskrit name Gokṣura, referring to its resemblance to a cow's hoof.
traditionalReferences:
Gokshura is an established Ayurvedic medicinal plant.
• Charaka Saṃhitā includes Gokṣura in classical medicinal groups.
• Suśruta Saṃhitā describes Gokṣura in contexts related to urinary and other conditions.
• Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya also includes it in medicinal formulations.
• It is an ingredient in several classical formulations associated with urinary and
reproductive health.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Urinary complaints
• Difficulty in urination
• Kidney and urinary tract-related preparations
• Swelling and fluid-related conditions
• Reproductive-health formulations
• General strengthening preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.

Modern research has investigated Tribulus terrestris for urinary, cardiovascular, antioxidant
and reproductive-related effects.

performance, clinical evidence does not consistently demonstrate significant testosterone-
boosting or muscle-building effects in healthy men.
Research results vary substantially depending on extract type and dose.

• Protodioscin
• Diosgenin
• Tribulosin
• Flavonoids

plants.safetySummary:
Gokshura is used traditionally, but concentrated extracts may have effects different from normal
dietary exposure. People with kidney, liver or cardiovascular conditions and those taking
medicines should consult a healthcare professional before using concentrated preparations.

containing small green seeds.

Mudga is extensively described as a food.

Gudmar is a woody climbing plant. Its leaves are opposite and oval/elliptical. Small greenish-
yellow flowers occur in clusters, followed by characteristic follicles.
The plant is famous for the traditional association of its leaves with reducing the perception of
sweetness.

Gudūcyādi Varga — verses 216–217
Verse 216 describes:
• Meṣaśṛṅgī
• Tikta rasa
• Ruksha nature
• Katu post-digestive effect
and traditional uses involving respiratory complaints, wounds, Kapha and eye-related pain.

Gudmar has traditionally been used in relation to:
• Meha

branched stem with narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged opposite each other. The flowers are

scientificEvidence:
Modern research on Azadirachta indica has investigated its antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory,
antioxidant, insecticidal and metabolic effects.
Antimicrobial activity: Laboratory and experimental studies have reported antibacterial,
antifungal, antiviral and antiparasitic activity from different neem extracts and compounds.
However, further research is required to establish the appropriate preparations, mechanisms,
safety and clinical effectiveness in humans.
Metabolic health: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical study involving 80
people with type 2 diabetes investigated a standardized aqueous extract of neem leaves and twigs
for 12 weeks. The study reported improvements in measures including fasting and post-meal
blood glucose, HbA1c and insulin resistance compared with placebo.
Another clinical study in people with metabolic syndrome also investigated different doses of an
aqueous neem leaf-and-twig extract and reported improvements in several metabolic and
endothelial-function measures.

findings, clinical research on Neem remains limited. Different studies use different plant parts,
extracts, doses and preparations. Therefore, Neem should not be presented as a clinically proven
treatment or cure for diseases.

Neem should not automatically be considered completely safe simply because it is a natural
plant.
Neem preparations can differ considerably depending on the plant part, concentration and
method of preparation. Neem oil ingestion has been associated with poisoning, particularly in
children, with reported effects including vomiting, metabolic disturbances and encephalopathy.
Concentrated extracts and supplements should therefore be used cautiously. Pregnant people,
children, people taking medicines and anyone considering concentrated oral neem preparations
should seek appropriate medical advice.

along the stem. The plant bears small flowers and develops small fruits.

plants.identification:
Sarpagandha is a small perennial evergreen shrub.
Its leaves are usually arranged in whorls around the stem. The leaves are simple, smooth and
elliptical to lance-shaped.
Flowers are small, usually white or pinkish. Fruits are small, rounded and become dark when
mature.
The root is long, cylindrical and characteristically twisted, with a brownish outer surface.
traditionalReferences:
Sarpagandha is particularly prominent in later Ayurvedic medicinal literature and Nighaṇṭu
traditions rather than being one of the major frequently cited plants of early Charaka
classifications.
For Jeevan Sutra, it is important not to manufacture a Charaka citation simply because the
plant is famous in Ayurveda. The database should identify the exact classical source when a
specific quotation is provided.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally associated with:
• Sleep-related preparations
• Mental restlessness
• Vāta-related conditions
• Traditional cardiovascular preparations
• Nervous-system-related conditions
• Certain formulations intended to promote calmness
scientificEvidence:
Sarpagandha became extremely important in modern pharmacology because its roots contain
indole alkaloids, particularly reserpine.
Reserpine affects the storage of neurotransmitters such as norepinephrine, dopamine and
serotonin in nerve cells. Historically, reserpine played an important role in the development of
modern antihypertensive therapy.
Other alkaloids such as ajmaline and ajmalicine have also been studied for cardiovascular and
neurological effects.
knownCompounds:
• Reserpine
• Rescinnamine
• Ajmaline
• Ajmalicine
• Serpentine
• Yohimbine
• Other indole alkaloids
plants.safetySummary:
Sarpagandha is pharmacologically active and should not be treated as an ordinary herbal
supplement.
Possible concerns include:
• Excessive lowering of blood pressure
• Drowsiness
• Depression-related effects
• Drug interactions
• Cardiovascular effects
It can interact with medicines used for blood pressure and nervous-system conditions.

Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Skin-related conditions
• Burning sensations
• Urinary complaints
• Inflammatory conditions
• Digestive complaints
• General cooling and restorative preparations

scientificEvidence:
Research on Hemidesmus indicus has investigated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory,
antimicrobial and hepatoprotective activities.

provide scientific interest in the plant, they do not by themselves establish effectiveness in
humans.

Sirish is a large deciduous or semi-evergreen tree that can grow approximately 15–25 metres tall.
It has a broad spreading crown and bipinnate leaves made up of many small leaflets.
Its flowers are pale greenish-yellow or cream-coloured and have numerous long stamens, giving

containing several seeds.
traditionalReferences:
Sirish is traditionally known as Śirīṣa and is particularly significant in Ayurveda.
• Charaka Saṃhitā includes Śirīṣa among important medicinal substances.
• It is especially associated with traditional management of Viṣa-related conditions
(poison/toxin-related contexts).
• Suśruta Saṃhitā also discusses Śirīṣa in relation to toxicological and medicinal
applications.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu describes Śirīṣa and its traditional properties.
The plant is particularly notable because it has a strong association with Agada Tantra, the
Ayurvedic branch dealing with poisons and toxic substances.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Poison/toxin-related traditional preparations
• Allergic-type complaints
• Skin-related conditions
• Respiratory complaints
• Inflammatory conditions
• Swelling and related traditional applications
• Various compound formulations
These are traditional Ayurvedic uses and should not be presented as proven antidotes or
treatments for poisoning.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research on Albizia lebbeck has investigated antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-
inflammatory and immunomodulatory activities.
Some experimental studies have also examined its possible effects on allergic and respiratory
pathways. However, much of this evidence comes from laboratory or animal studies, and there is
insufficient clinical evidence to establish Sirish as an effective treatment or antidote for
poisoning.

• Tannins
• Flavonoids
• Alkaloids
• Terpenoids
• Phenolic compounds
• Various glycosides

pharmacological effects. Because it has traditionally been associated with toxicological
preparations, it is particularly important not to describe it as a substitute for emergency
treatment after poisoning or envenomation.

compound leaves. The flowers are large and generally purple, maroon or reddish-purple. Its

Gudūcyādi Varga — verses 22–23

and kāsa.

• Swelling/inflammatory conditions
• Respiratory complaints
• Cough
• Digestive disturbances
• Conditions associated with Vata and Kapha
• Preparations containing Dashamula

plants.safetySummary:

preparations should be used appropriately rather than assuming that a larger dose is better.

plants.identification:
Shatavari is a perennial, climbing herb with slender stems and small, needle-like structures. It
produces small, fragrant flowers followed by berries. The plant develops numerous fleshy,
tuberous roots, which are the principal medicinal part traditionally used.
traditionalReferences:
Shatavari is an established medicinal plant in classical Ayurveda and is described particularly in
relation to women's health, nourishment and Rasayana use.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Shatavari has been used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Women's reproductive health
• Supporting lactation
• Digestive complaints
• Gastric discomfort and ulcers
• General nourishment and strength
• Rejuvenative (Rasayana) preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research on Asparagus racemosus has investigated its possible reproductive,
gastrointestinal, antioxidant and immunomodulatory effects.
Women's health: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical study involving 70
women reported improvements in several menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, night
sweats, insomnia and anxiety, with the studied Shatavari formulation. No significant adverse
events were recorded during the study.
Recent evidence: A 2025 multicenter randomized, double-blind study involving 135 women
aged 45–65 years examined Shatavari alone and in combination with Ashwagandha for
menopausal symptoms. The study reported improvements in several outcomes, but the authors
noted that longer and larger studies are needed.
Other research: Experimental and earlier clinical research has investigated possible
gastrointestinal, antioxidant and immunomodulatory activities, but evidence for many traditional
applications remains limited or preliminary.
Evidence limitation: Studies differ in the plant preparation, extract, dose and population
studied. Therefore, these findings do not establish Shatavari as a treatment or cure for disease.
knownCompounds:
Shatavari contains several bioactive compounds, including:
• Shatavarins I–IV
• Steroidal saponins
• Flavonoids
• Polysaccharides
• Other phytochemicals
Steroidal saponins, particularly shatavarins, are among the major constituents studied in
Shatavari roots.
plants.safetySummary:
Shatavari has generally shown good tolerability in available studies, but evidence on long-term
human safety remains limited.
Some studies have reported mild adverse effects such as gastrointestinal symptoms. Because
concentrated extracts may have biological effects and may interact with medicines, people taking
medicines or using concentrated supplements should seek appropriate medical advice.

plants.identification:
Sesame is an annual herb generally growing around 50–150 cm tall. It has erect stems, opposite
or alternate leaves and tubular flowers that may be white, pink or purple. The plant produces
elongated capsules containing numerous small seeds.
The seeds may be white, cream, brown or black depending on the variety. Sesame oil is obtained
by pressing or processing the seeds.
traditionalReferences:
Sesame is one of the important classical oils and medicinal substances in Ayurveda and is
known as Tila.
• Charaka Saṃhitā describes Tila and Tila Taila in several contexts.
• Suśruta Saṃhitā also gives sesame oil an important role in traditional external and
internal preparations.
• Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya describes the traditional properties and applications of sesame oil.
• Sesame oil is particularly important in traditional Snehana (oleation) practices.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Oil massage and external oleation
• Dryness-related conditions
• Musculoskeletal preparations
• Skin care
• Hair and scalp applications
• Certain oral and dental practices
• Nutritional and strengthening preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Sesame seeds and sesame oil have been studied for their antioxidant, lipid-related and anti-
inflammatory properties.
Sesame contains lignans and unsaturated fatty acids that may contribute to its biological activity.
Human studies have investigated sesame consumption and oil in relation to blood pressure, lipid
profiles and oxidative stress, although results vary and study quality differs.
knownCompounds:
Sesame contains:
• Sesamin
• Sesamolin
• Sesamol
• Oleic acid
• Linoleic acid
• Tocopherols
• Phytosterols
• Protein and dietary fibre
Sesamin and sesamolin are characteristic lignans of sesame.
plants.safetySummary:
Sesame is a common food, but sesame allergy can be severe in susceptible individuals. Sesame
oil used topically may also cause skin reactions in some people.
Normal dietary use and concentrated medicinal preparations should be distinguished.

Shalmali is a large deciduous tree, often with a tall trunk covered with large conical prickles
when young. It produces large, bright red flowers, especially when the tree is leafless.
Its fruits are large capsules containing numerous seeds surrounded by silky cotton-like fibres.
traditionalReferences:
Charaka Saṃhitā
Shalmali occurs in:
• Purīṣavirajanīya
• Śoṇitasthāpana
• Vedanasthāpana
• Kaṣāya Skandha
The Charaka database records traditional applications including Raktapitta, Vrana and Daha.
Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu
The cited edition gives:
Gudūcyādi Varga — verses 54–55
The description gives synonyms such as:
• Mocha
• Picchila
• Purani
• Raktapuṣpa
• Sthirāyu
• Kaṇṭakādhya
• Tūlinī
and describes Shalmali as cooling, sweet and traditionally useful in Vata-Pitta conditions.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in contexts involving:
• Raktapitta — bleeding disorders
• Wounds
• Burning sensation
• Haemorrhoids
• Excessive Pitta
• Certain gastrointestinal complaints
• Traditional rejuvenative preparations
Shalmali flowers are specifically described as astringent and are mentioned in the context of

scientificEvidence:
Modern studies of Bombax ceiba have investigated:

• Anti-inflammatory activity
• Antimicrobial activity
• Hepatoprotective effects

treated as one uniform preparation. Clinical dosage and safety information for concentrated
extracts remain limited.

plants.identification:
Vidarikand is a large perennial climbing or twining plant. It has trifoliate leaves, with broad
leaflets, and produces clusters of purple or bluish flowers.
The plant develops large underground tubers that can become considerably enlarged. These
tubers are the principal medicinal part and are traditionally dried and powdered for formulations.
traditionalReferences:
Vidari is traditionally known as Vidārī and is regarded as a nourishing and strengthening
medicinal plant.
• Classical Ayurvedic literature describes Vidārī in nutritional and restorative contexts.
• Charaka Saṃhitā includes Vidārī-related substances in traditional formulations.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu describes Vidārī and its traditional properties.
• It is associated with Bṛṃhaṇa (nourishing/strengthening) preparations.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in contexts related to:
• General weakness
• Nutritional and strengthening preparations
• Rejuvenative formulations
• Digestive and restorative preparations
• Reproductive-health-related formulations
• Traditional preparations intended to support vitality
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Research on Pueraria tuberosa has investigated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, metabolic
and reproductive-related biological activities.
Studies have identified several phytochemicals and explored their effects in laboratory and
animal models. However, clinical evidence in humans remains limited, and traditional claims
about strength, fertility or vitality should not be presented as established medical effects.
knownCompounds:
Vidarikand contains:
• Puerarin
• Daidzein
• Genistein
• Tuberostan
• Isoflavonoids
• Triterpenoids
• Various phenolic compounds
plants.safetySummary:
Vidarikand has a history of traditional use, but concentrated extracts may have biological effects
that differ from normal dietary use. Because it contains phytoestrogenic isoflavonoids, people
with hormone-sensitive conditions or those taking hormone-related medicines should seek
professional advice before using concentrated preparations.

plants.identification:
Vidanga is a woody climbing or scrambling shrub found in tropical and subtropical regions. Its
leaves are simple, leathery and generally elliptical.
The plant produces small flowers followed by small round fruits. The dried fruits are dark brown
to black and have a characteristic appearance resembling small peppercorns.
traditionalReferences:
Vidanga is an important classical Ayurvedic herb.
• Charaka Saṃhitā includes Vidanga in traditional medicinal classifications.
• Suśruta Saṃhitā describes it in medicinal contexts.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu provides a detailed description of Vidanga.
• Its Sanskrit name Krimighna reflects its traditional association with intestinal “krimi” or
worms.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Intestinal worm-related preparations
• Digestive complaints
• Loss of appetite
• Abdominal discomfort
• Skin-related conditions
• Cleansing and digestive formulations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven antiparasitic treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Vidanga has been investigated experimentally for anthelmintic, antimicrobial, antioxidant
and anti-inflammatory activities.
Its traditional association with intestinal worms has led researchers to study its extracts against
parasites in laboratory and animal models. However, clinical evidence in humans is limited, and
it should not be presented as a substitute for established antiparasitic medicines.
knownCompounds:
Vidanga contains:
• Embelin
• Embelin-related quinones
• Rapanone
• Vilanin
• Tannins
• Other phenolic compounds
Embelin is considered one of the principal bioactive constituents.
plants.safetySummary:
Concentrated Vidanga preparations should be used carefully. High doses may cause
gastrointestinal effects, and safety during pregnancy has not been adequately established.

plants.scientificName: Crataeva nurvala Buch.-Ham. / Crataeva religiosa Forssk.
plants.identification:
Varuna is a small-to-medium tree with trifoliate leaves, meaning each leaf has three leaflets.
It produces fragrant flowers that may be white initially and become yellowish/reddish with age.
traditionalReferences:
Charaka Saṃhitā
Varuna is recorded in:
• Sūtra Sthāna 14/31 — Nāḍī Sveda
• Śarīra Sthāna 8/33
• Cikitsā Sthāna 3/267
• Cikitsā Sthāna 5/165 — Pathya in Gulma
• Cikitsā Sthāna 14/45 — Svedana
Therapeutic associations
Classical descriptions particularly associate Varuna with:
• Aśmarī — urinary stones
• Mūtrakṛcchra — painful/difficult urination
• Gulma
• Vidradhi — abscess
traditionalUses:
Especially important traditionally in:
• Urinary disorders
• Urinary stone-related conditions
• Difficulty in urination
• Abdominal masses/Gulma
• Swelling
• Certain inflammatory conditions
scientificEvidence:
Modern research has investigated Crataeva species particularly for urolithiasis/urinary stone-
related activity, as well as:
• Anti-inflammatory effects
• Antioxidant activity
• Antimicrobial effects
• Diuretic activity
Experimental findings are promising but should not be represented as proof that Varuna
dissolves stones in every patient.

• Lupeol
• Betulin
• β-sitosterol
• Flavonoids
• Triterpenoids
• Saponins
plants.safetySummary:
Urinary stones can cause obstruction and kidney injury. Varuna should therefore not be
presented as a replacement for medical evaluation, particularly when there is severe pain,
fever, vomiting or urinary obstruction.

plants.identification:
Vacha is a perennial aromatic herb that grows mainly in wet or marshy areas. It has long, narrow,
sword-shaped leaves arising from an underground rhizome.
The rhizome is thick, aromatic and yellowish-brown on the outside. Small flowers are arranged
closely on a cylindrical spike called a spadix.
traditionalReferences:
Vacha is a classical Ayurvedic medicinal plant.
• Charaka Saṃhitā describes Vacā in several medicinal contexts.
• Suśruta Saṃhitā also includes it among medicinal substances.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu describes its traditional properties.
• It has traditionally been associated with speech, memory, digestion and respiratory
preparations.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in contexts related to:
• Speech-related preparations
• Memory and cognition
• Digestive complaints
• Cough and respiratory conditions
• Abdominal discomfort
• Traditional nervous-system preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Research has investigated Acorus calamus for antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory
and neuroactive properties.
However, Vacha is an especially important example where botanical chemistry and safety
matter. Some varieties and preparations contain β-asarone, a compound that has raised
significant toxicological concerns.
knownCompounds:
Vacha contains:
• α-Asarone
• β-Asarone
• Eugenol
• Acorenone
• Other volatile-oil constituents
The concentration of β-asarone can vary significantly depending on the plant variety and
geographic origin.
plants.safetySummary:
This plant needs special caution. β-Asarone has been associated with toxicological concerns,
including potential carcinogenicity in experimental studies. Therefore, concentrated oral
preparations of Acorus calamus should not be casually recommended.
For your app, don't write simply “Vacha is safe.” The species/chemotype and preparation matter
considerably.

plants.identification:
Turmeric is a perennial herb with long, broad green leaves arising from underground rhizomes. It
produces pale yellow to yellowish-white flowers. The rhizome is bright yellow-orange inside and
has a characteristic aroma.
traditionalReferences: Turmeric, known as Haridrā, is described in classical Ayurvedic literature.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, turmeric rhizome has been used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Skin health
• Wound care
• Digestive health
• Inflammatory conditions
• Respiratory complaints
• General medicinal and dietary preparations
These represent traditional uses and should not automatically be interpreted as scientifically
proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Turmeric has been extensively studied because its rhizome contains curcuminoids, particularly
curcumin.
Inflammation: Laboratory and clinical research suggests that curcumin can influence several
molecular pathways involved in inflammation. Some clinical studies have reported
improvements in inflammatory markers, although results vary depending on the formulation and
dose.
Osteoarthritis: Several randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews have investigated
curcumin preparations for osteoarthritis-related pain and function. Some studies suggest modest
improvement in pain and physical function, but the quality and formulations of studies vary.
Antioxidant activity: Curcumin has demonstrated antioxidant activity in laboratory and
experimental studies. It can interact with pathways involved in oxidative stress.
Important limitation: Curcumin has low natural bioavailability, meaning relatively little is
absorbed into the bloodstream. Different formulations are therefore being studied to improve
absorption. Evidence for turmeric/curcumin should not be interpreted as proof that it can cure
diseases.
plants.safetySummary:
Turmeric used normally as a food spice is generally considered safe for most people. However,
concentrated curcumin/turmeric supplements can have stronger effects and may cause
gastrointestinal problems or interact with medicines. Rare cases of liver injury have been
reported with some highly bioavailable curcumin products. High-dose supplementation should
therefore not be treated as equivalent to ordinary dietary use.
Turmeric (Curcuma longa), known as Haridrā in Ayurveda, is an important medicinal and
culinary plant whose rhizome has been traditionally used in various Ayurvedic preparations.
Modern research has particularly focused on its curcuminoids, especially curcumin, and their
possible anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. Clinical evidence is promising for some
applications, such as osteoarthritis symptoms, but further high-quality research is needed.

plants.identification:
Tulsi is an erect, highly branched, aromatic herb. It generally grows about 30–60 cm tall and has
hairy stems and leaves. The leaves may be green or purplish depending on the variety. It
produces small flowers arranged in elongated spikes.
traditionalReferences: Tulsi is referred to as Tulasī and Surasā in Ayurvedic literature.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally, Tulsi has been used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Cough
• Breathing difficulties
• Rhinitis and nasal complaints
• Digestive complaints
• Skin-related conditions
• Certain microbial/parasitic conditions
• General medicinal preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
plants.safetySummary:
Tulsi has been used traditionally as a food and medicinal herb, but concentrated extracts and
supplements should not automatically be considered risk-free. Human studies have generally
reported good tolerability, although adverse effects have occasionally been reported. People
taking medicines or using concentrated supplements should seek appropriate medical advice.

Yashtimadhu is a perennial herb with underground roots and stolons. Its roots are yellowish
inside and have a naturally sweet taste. The plant has pinnate leaves with several leaflets and
small flowers arranged in clusters.
traditionalReferences:
Yashtimadhu is a well-established Ayurvedic medicinal plant.
• Charaka Saṃhitā — includes Yashtimadhu in several traditional classifications.
• Suśruta Saṃhitā — includes it in Kakolyādi-related groups.
• Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu — describes Yaṣṭimadhu and its properties.
traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in Ayurveda in contexts related to:
• Cough and throat complaints
• Digestive discomfort
• Inflammatory conditions
• Voice-related preparations
• Skin-related conditions
• General strengthening and restorative preparations
These are traditional uses and should not be presented as proven treatments.
scientificEvidence:
Modern research has investigated licorice for gastrointestinal, inflammatory and other biological

• Glycyrrhetinic acid
• Glabridin

potassium levels and high blood pressure and may produce other complications. Therefore,
concentrated preparations should be used cautiously.

plants.identification:
Vijaysar is a large deciduous tree. It has compound leaves, yellow flowers and characteristic
woody fruits.
The heartwood is the principal medicinal part traditionally used.
traditionalReferences:
Vijaysar is also known under names such as Asana and Bijaka in classical literature.
A classical verse recorded for Asana/Bijaka is:

“बीजकः पीतसारश्च पीतशालक इत्यवप ।

Kapha/Pitta-related conditions.

• Sushruta — Sālasārādi Gana
• Vagbhata — Asanādi Gana

traditionalUses:
Traditionally used in contexts involving:
• Prameha
• Madhumeha
• Excess Kapha and Meda
• Certain skin disorders
• Wounds
• Digestive/metabolic complaints

Modern research has particularly investigated Pterocarpus marsupium for antidiabetic and

for modern standardized extracts.

• Pterosupin
